paragraphs.text: XIII. ON THE SINGLE LIFE OF THE CLERGY.

Some time ago, dearest sons, I promised you a letter that would draw on the law to commend the rules for every kind of conduct, and would set out in summary everything that applies generally to all clerics in directing their discipline. But now certain of you have sunk into public disgrace by living with women, so the Lord's rebuke has compelled me to write to you specifically about this matter as well. Because of your negligence he has ordered me, wretched as I am, to issue a fittingly severe command that clerics are not to live with women. This admonition would be enough on the authority of my letter alone. Yet so that no one may laugh at me as a dreamer, as his brothers laughed at Joseph, we add the firm support of the Scriptures. Then all may know that by revelation the Lord now commands what the Scriptures show he had already commanded before. They may also know that we are not adulterating the word of the Lord, nor boastfully seeking to glory in revelations, but that we speak as in the Lord's sight and do not lie in what we say. We are confident that we have heard no falsehood from the Lord, and we rely on the voice of the apostle Paul, who declares: "For we are not like so many, adulterating the word of God; but we speak in Christ out of sincerity, as from God and before him." We are in the deepest grief over certain wasted members of our body, and we groan at the loss suffered by the church, which mourns as our sloth reduces it day by day to a pitiful few. Still, we believe we are relieved in some measure because the negligence of certain people cannot harm our diligence. They have never lacked letters from us, and the frequency of those letters has made up to everyone for my absence. Let everyone who scorns this write himself down as guilty of his own disregard. With an open face we cry out to the scorners what Solomon confidently reproaches: "Because I called," he says, "and you did not obey; I stretched out my words, and you paid no attention; you made my counsels void and gave no heed to my rebukes. Therefore I too will laugh at your destruction. I will rejoice over you when ruin comes upon you, when sudden turmoil comes upon you and overthrow like a storm, when distress and siege come upon you. For when you call on me, I will not hear you. The wicked will seek me and will not find me, for they hated wisdom. They did not take up the word of the Lord, nor were they willing to heed my counsels. They spurned my reproofs, and so they will eat the fruit of their own way and be filled with their own ungodliness."

Our exhortation now turns to you, whom we do not want to see experience such headlong falls into ruin. Fear the destruction of such a fall as much as you can, and let the examples of those who have slipped and been overthrown terrify us. Anyone who presses on across the same ground after seeing another fall there is far too reckless. Anyone who is not struck with fear when another perishes is utterly unbridled. The one who truly loves his own safety avoids running into another man's death. The prudent man becomes anxious at the disasters of others, as Solomon confirms when he says: "When the wicked man is punished, the shrewd man who sees it will be greatly instructed," and again: "When the ungodly fall, the righteous will be greatly afraid." It is a hostile kind of confidence that entrusts its life to dangers as if it were safe. It is a slippery hope that expects to be saved amid the kindling of sin. Victory is uncertain when one fights among enemy weapons, and it is impossible to be surrounded by flames and not burn. Solomon denies it, saying: "Who can bind fire in his bosom and not burn his clothes? Or who can walk on burning coals and not burn his feet? So it is with the man who goes in to his neighbor's wife: he will not go unpunished, nor will anyone who touches her." Believe, I beg you, believe the faithfulness of God rather than your own, for nothing he promises can deceive. The Lord says: "It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fall." And again: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." So we deceive ourselves whenever our belief is disordered, and we suppose that our faith can change the precepts of the law, so that we hope chastity can be kept unshaken wherever men and women mingle.

Hardly anyone can drink poison and live. A man asleep on a riverbank should fear falling in, for the apostle says: "Let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." In this matter it is better to fear wisely than to trust foolishly. It is more useful for a man to know he is weak and so prove strong than to want to seem strong and turn out weak. On this point the apostle rebukes the presumptuous, saying: "If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself." The self-deceiver certainly deceives his own soul when he fails to guard against harmful things and puts himself in their way. The man who looks after himself more safely is always wary of evil and fears every harmful appearance. Solomon set out the difference between the two, saying: "The wise man fears and turns away from all evil, but the fool trusts in himself and mingles with the wicked." Divine wisdom has found a great plan by which fear helps to set us free. Providence has great shortcuts, so that virtue and victory sometimes come through fear. The Lord has granted great remedies for salvation, so that even the fearful man may have praise, as Solomon says again: "Blessed is the man who reveres all things through fear." The Lord's mercy is beyond measure, for it has given glory to his people from every side. His kindness is beyond understanding, for it awards palms to match the battles. By confidence we overcome the savagery of men, and by fear we conquer the allurements of women. In this way the Lord works glories in us out of both strength and weakness, so that in all things and through all things he shows himself almighty. He assigns different kinds of triumph, so that we win our wars by counsel as much as by strength. Thus, contrary to Solomon, the works of wisdom would not be made empty if we were to conquer by the strength of faith alone. Now, then, the arms of wisdom must be carried where the female and male sexes declare war on each other. That is why Solomon gives this instruction: "Make prudence known to you, so that it may keep you from the strange and wicked woman." See now that in this war we have been given prudence as our conqueror, not faith, and prudence sets us free through the remedy of timidity. Consider which weapons must be taken up now, if you want the help of the law. Be fearful so that you may be fearless. Fear may seem a weakness in battle, yet according to the apostle's word, strength is made perfect in weakness. Separate yourselves, I beg you, separate yourselves from this pestilent contagion.

The farther each person is from adversity, the less he feels it. A man is less goaded by pleasures when he is not where pleasures abound. A man suffers less from the troubles of avarice when he does not see riches, if we accept the apostle's assurance: "Those who want to become rich," he says, "fall into temptation and a snare and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a man into ruin and destruction." In the same way, a man joined to a woman is exposed to temptations, for in her there is nothing but what wounds whoever comes near. The female form has become the sting of sin, and the condition of death arose from no other source than woman's substance. Solomon recalls this to make us vigilant, saying: "Sin had its beginning from a woman, and because of her we all die." That is why we are held mortal, and yet we do not fear. What would we do if we were already immortal? Christ has indeed set us free through a woman, but we must still dread that which still causes our death. Our deliverance through a woman will be complete only when we in turn conquer the death that came through a woman. Otherwise, if temptations still rule around us through woman, we have surely squandered the deliverance Christ gave. For this hope of freedom, which we believe Christ granted to our faith, still lies in the future: then woman will not harm us at all, when death itself has been abolished. If we think we are already beyond the reach of women's darts, then nothing is left for the heavenly kingdom. The apostle rightly rebukes such thinking, saying: "Already you are filled, already you have become rich; without us you reign, and would that you did reign!" The time of struggle is still going on, and death through woman still rages. I would be lying if I said we do not see many people destroyed by it. How many bishops and clerics, and laypeople too, and men of what standing, had fought through the contests of confession and won their victories, had shown mighty works, signs and wonders everywhere? Yet they are known to have been shipwrecked with all of these, because they wanted to sail in a fragile ship. How many lions has one delicate weakness tamed? Though it is cheap and wretched, it makes prey of the great. Solomon speaks of this, saying: "The price of a harlot is as much as a single loaf, but a woman captures precious souls."

These things are happening before our very eyes, and still no terrors restrain us. What would we do if we only heard of past events by rumor? But this is always the unbelief of hardened human nature. Neither hearing nor even seeing convinces it that others have perished, unless it sees itself perishing too. The deaths of its companions do not shake it, because it supposes they deserved it or were weak. It confidently thinks itself very deserving or very strong, unaware that when punishments fall on some, an example is being given to all. The Lord sets this out in the gospel and says: "Do you think that these Galileans who suffered such things were worse sinners than all the other Galileans? No, I tell you; unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way, like those on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them. Do you think that they too were greater debtors than all the other people living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; if you do not repent, you will all perish in the same way."

We wonder that Adam was led astray through Eve, yet no examples of people dying had gone before him, and only a single command bound him. Now neither countless deaths nor endless commands restrain us. To us this may fittingly be said, after the pattern of the Lord's rebuke: "If Adam had seen the deaths that have taken place among you, he would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Adam on the day of judgment than for you." Far away, very far away, let this plague, this pestilence, this hidden ruin be! Oh, how disordered is closeness to a woman! [?] The brigandage of sins hurls its darts at whoever she is near. There can be no honest sincerity in this companionship, for it is full of clashes, as if tossed by turbulent waves. Friendly harmony does not live in this intimacy, since it produces nothing but discord and hostility. The Lord did make woman a helper for man, but through the serpent's envy she took on the part of an enemy. If the woman who was born from her own husband tempts to this day the very man to whom she is joined, how much more will a woman do so who is coupled with a man by no lawful bond? If those who have grown together as two in one flesh prick one another with mutual temptations, what will those do who were neither born in one flesh nor joined in it? Above all, the man drawn away by love for another is no longer able even to call upon God. The man who has found someone to look after at home is not allowed to think about divine things. For this reason the apostle advises: "I want you to be free from anxiety. The man who has no wife is anxious about how to please God; but the man who has a wife thinks about the things of this world, how to please his wife." What is there to delight in such a union, which holds nothing but battles? Or what benefit does it offer, when there are no marital duties, since even those cannot be free of danger? Everything about a woman is an occasion of trouble, and union with her is always hostile. By its bond it causes great distress, and on the man it clings to unlawfully it inflicts an incurable wound. Sparks leap from coals, rust feeds on iron, asps hiss out sickness, and woman pours out the pestilence of lust. Solomon makes this comparison, saying: "From garments comes the moth, and from a woman a man's wickedness."
I want to know what this shared affection is, and what this sickness of discord is.

…is always ambiguous, and by attacking its own purpose with wavering counsels throws it into confusion. Why has a man who scorned to marry a wife taken a woman to himself? If anyone will not eat meat, why does he fill his dwelling with dishes of meat? And if he will not drink wine, why does he take his pleasure in wine? As if the mind were not sometimes fed by a plenty of food merely by having it, without tasting it, and as if the mind were not often stirred by the mere fragrance of scented wine! Why does he want, through hypocrisy, to be called abstinent by men, while in secret he is stuffed with meat and drunkenness? Many have riches which they deny to their own use but keep out of greed; if no greed clung to them, they would not possess the trappings of greed. But because they are possessed by greed, they enjoy in their minds what they do not touch in use. So too the man who has spurned the bond of marriage is bound in another way by the bonds of a woman: though he joins with her in no intercourse, he is still always delighted by desire, by sight, by conversation, by companionship. For if he had no desire for a woman, he would never take a woman for his delight. Indeed, he has given me a still more suspicious impression, since he took one who was not lawful and refused the lawful one: unless I am mistaken, he has contrived to promise holiness to men in public and in secret not to be without a wife. Two pretences, one of lust and one of holiness, are to be wondered at here, each covering the other and each betraying the other. This ingenious eunuch-and-adulterer works against himself while he schemes, and while he seeks both. He has achieved neither, so that he is by no means reckoned holy, though he does not enjoy a true union; for the apostle Paul says: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.” But I grant that the purity of this chastity has not been violated; yet he offers an evil report to the suspicious, and in vain guards within, by laborious struggle, the good of purity which outwardly he causes to be defamed. He thus overturns the teaching of the apostle Paul, who both foresees and warns: “Why,” he says, “is my liberty judged by an unbelieving conscience? If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks?” It is worse than adultery to make continence criminal and holiness infamous. Whoever does not fulfil before everyone what he professes heaps blasphemy on the religion he has embraced; what is professed must be fulfilled openly, lest Christianity be believed to be a deception and adultery seem to be clothed in the veil of holiness. For this reason the Lord forewarns us in the gospel, saying: “Let your light so shine before men, that seeing your good works they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.” The apostle Paul follows this too, saying: “Let not your good, then, be blasphemed.” And again: “Providing things that are good not only before God but also before men.” And in another place: “Whether, then, you eat or drink or do anything else, do all things to the glory of God, and be without offence to Jews and Greeks and to the church of God, just as I too please all men in all things.”

But perhaps the objection is raised: what of the fact that he himself said elsewhere, “If I wished to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ”? The sayings of the law never exclude one another; rather, every one of its answers is fixed to its proper place. It is not permitted to please men in a case where the will of men does not admit the will of the Lord; but where men accept what advances the glory of God, the apostle Paul himself commanded that it be made known to all. “Let each of us,” he says, “please his neighbour for his good edification.” How far, then, can he expect the reward of holiness who not only provokes unbelievers to blaspheme holiness but also offers a ruinous example to believers? The result is that the weak, under the pretext of love, commit fornication in a subtle way, and the “chaste” man gives a most unchaste lesson in chastity, overturning what the apostle Paul threatens: “Shall the weak brother perish through your knowledge, for whose sake Christ suffered? When you sin in this way against the brothers and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.” And indeed it befits not only the young but the old as well to have regard for the weakness of the brothers, lest old age, from which all wholesome teaching ought to proceed, lead youth to perish. So Eleazar declares in the book of Maccabees, saying: “I would rather be sent ahead to the underworld [than desert the laws of our fathers]. For it is not worthy of our age to pretend, lest many of the young, thinking that Eleazar at ninety years of age had gone over to the way of life of foreigners, should themselves be led astray through me, because of my pretence and for the sake of a brief and perishable span of life, and I should bring hatred and disgrace upon my old age.” He chose to throw his life to torments rather than be anyone's teacher of perdition; and we, where there are no torments, are unwilling to put the brothers who are to be saved ahead of mere fleeting pleasures, nor are we content to benefit ourselves and others alike without any tortures at all, when he refused to live even though he was to die for it, as he went on to say further below: “Therefore by departing this life bravely I shall show myself worthy of my old age, and I shall leave to the young a noble example, so that with ready mind and with courage they may depart by an honourable death for the weighty and holy laws.” Though this befits lay people too, so that they do not offer outsiders occasions for blasphemy or the brotherhood an opportunity for fornication, this necessity binds clerics above all and most strictly, for on them either a blasphemed religion or a ruined brotherhood will inflict a double penalty. Nor will those who have supplied the tinder of sin to foreigners and brothers find any comfort at all in the Lord's judgment. For this reason the apostle Paul instructs Titus thus: “Showing yourself an example of good works in teaching, in integrity, in seriousness, in sound and irreproachable speech, so that the adversary may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say of us.” And again: “Show good faith to all,” he says, “so that in all things they may display the good teaching of our Lord the Saviour.” So too he writes to Timothy, saying: “Be a pattern to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in chastity.” The apostle Peter fully confirms this, saying: “Let your conduct among the Gentiles be good, so that in the very thing in which they speak against us as evildoers, they may glorify the Lord because of your good works.” And again: “For such,” he says, “is the will of God, that by doing good you may silence the ignorance of foolish men.”

Nor let anyone propose to himself and say: “I want to have something to overcome.” For that is to say: “I desire to live beneath a collapsing house.” Who is so foolish as to wish to be pressed into toil when he is offered a more comfortable triumph? For it is no double triumph to be proved a victor in the presence of a woman rather than to keep intact in solitude the pledge of holiness. And since there is one and the same title of glory, the strong man who toils hard is in this case labouring in vain, and is rewarded equally with the one who has won with little toil. What of the fact that he, rather, is counted as perfect who shows himself cut off in every respect from womanly affections? For the Lord in the gospel calls him perfect who has cut off his whole patrimony from his own use. Certainly, even for anyone living alone daily triumphs for chastity are not lacking, since the human body never ceases to assail the spirit with carnal desires, as the apostle affirms, saying: “The flesh,” he says, “lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish.” You already have your own flesh, which you must constantly overcome: why do you want to hire another as well? No one wishes to add a worse fever on top of the one he has, lest he begin to suffer from an incurable semitertian fever which no physician can relieve. Nor does anyone take up another's load on top of his own, lest, crushed by two burdens, he be sunk down to the underworld. Hence Jeremiah the prophet teaches that the weight of holiness must be borne alone: “It is good for a man,” he says, “when he has borne a heavy yoke in his youth: he will sit alone and keep silence, because he has taken the heavy yoke upon himself.”

But some malicious follower may take refuge in the saying of the apostle Paul: “Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ.” These are not the burdens which the apostle Paul commands us to carry. Rather, he means that as we bear with one another no discord should divide us, and that we should give mutual help to brothers who are in temptation—not that we should procure temptations for ourselves through women, but rather that we should lighten the weight of temptations. For he knows what the yoke of holiness is: that it can scarcely be borne even alone. On this point not only he but the Lord too refused to lay down a fixed precept, saying: “Not all can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given.” And again: “Let him who can receive it, receive it.” If, then, the greatness of this weight is borne with difficulty by a man alone, how will it be borne if it is made heavier by a doubled weight? And if almost all who live alone can scarcely hold out against the snares of the flesh, what will become of those who do not hesitate to throw themselves on swords hanging over them on both sides? I say more. If husbands and wives, who fulfil their conjugal desires every day, do not find that enough, what are those to do who join themselves to women only to increase their assaults? A woman's glance, meeting a man unexpectedly or in passing for a moment, shoots arrows, as it were, into another's eyes. If simple reverence is not free from danger then, what goes on where a woman, sharing the same dwelling, takes on the boldness of familiarity? When in her household work she now bares her arms and thighs at spinning wool, now, overheated, uncovers her limbs, now, tired out, tosses about, or sometimes dissolves into laughter, now offers endearments, and—what is more poisonous than all—delights to sing psalms or songs? It is more bearable to hear a basilisk hissing than to hear her singing. Solomon makes us wary of such a woman, saying: “Do not keep company with a dancing woman, nor listen to her, lest you perish by her power.” I pass over the rest, which are more to be blushed at than told; I say only this: to see a woman broken by grief or anger is already not without its allure. What shall we say if you see her merry, or, what is worse, caressing? Let me say it once for all: every unfitting companionship with women is a glue of sins and a poisoned birdlime with which the devil goes fowling. The company of women is unsuitable, and Solomon again teaches us to guard against their companionship in every way: “Do not sit at all,” he says, “with another man's wife, and do not quarrel with her over wine, lest perhaps your heart incline towards her and with your blood you slip into perdition.”

Finally, even if we are confident that our own mind will always stand firm in this shared life, at least this ought to make us wary: that the very women who live with us may perhaps be moved towards us, or, because of their impetuous youth, be goaded by frenzied incitements to other loves. Then, what is worse, we shall be the cause, through no cause of our own, of being stained by another's fornication—we in whose house others are offered the opportunity of a brothel—and we shall be swallowed up in the charge of another's guilt, since we ourselves arranged the procuring of that uncleanness. For this reason the apostle Paul instructs us about such matters, saying: “If your brother is offended because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not destroy with your food him for whom Christ died.” And again: “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine, or anything by which your brother stumbles or is offended or made weak.” And in another place: “Judge this rather,” he says, “that you put no stumbling block or occasion of offence before a brother.” And of himself he says: “Therefore, if food offends my brother, I will never eat meat again, lest I offend my brother.” When, therefore, the detestable trouble of this kind of union assails us, even if it cannot make us adulterers, it still makes us pimps for adulterers and the incestuous. For who, as a searcher of another's heart, could weigh the character of each person, and presume to fight against Satan on another's behalf and to be a fit guarantor before God? He is mad who promises anything about himself, not to say if he should even seem to stand surety for a woman, when the apostle Paul declares of himself: “Not that I have already received it, or am already justified, or already perfect; but I press on, if I may lay hold of that for which I was also laid hold of by Christ. Brothers, I do not consider that I have yet laid hold of it; but one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and reaching out to what lies ahead, I press on by the rule towards the prize of the upward calling of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let all of us, then, who are perfect think this way.” And again: “For me,” he says, “it is a very small thing to be judged by you or by any human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself. It is the Lord who judges me.” And in another place: “Blessed,” he says, “is the one who does not judge himself in the matter in which he tests another.” So, although we have nothing certain even about our own steadfastness, we who are ceaselessly tossed among the waves of the world, enduring its stormy onslaughts, yet if anyone has such confidence in the immovability of his own firmness, let him at least anxiously dread becoming a stumbling block in the eyes of others, and let him be terrified by the voice of the Lord threatening: “Woe,” he says, “to this world because of offences; but woe to that man through whom the offence comes.” If we fear and revere these threats of the Lord with a devout heart, let us dread our danger more on account of others than on our own account, since we are bound by the apostle Paul to serve one another's good. “Each of you,” he says, “considering not his own interests, but those of others.” And again: “Let no one seek his own good, but that of another.”

But someone seizes on something from Paul himself to object: “Each of us,” he says, “will give account of himself to God,” and “each will carry his own load.” Then let the man who does not want to give account for another not take an unlawful part in that other's affairs or business; and let the man who tries to be free and exempt from others' loads keep nothing belonging to another in his charge, which would put him under the opposite rule. For whoever has handled another's business must be subject to the other's account. The man in whose house a brother's loads have been lost through unsafe keeping must be held liable for the loss or the cost of the loads; for whatever in our house was under inadequate guard, or was broken into by thieves, is our responsibility, and whatever was badly kept through our negligence is required of us. Only then are we free of one another, if nothing of another's property is kept with us.

Perhaps someone may say: “Then we ought not even to gather together at the house of prayer, lest someone cause another to stumble?” This slanderous objection belongs to a heretical profession, which uses good things as a pretext to assert evil ones, prejudges holiness in order to introduce uncleanness subtly, and turns what is lawful into slander so as to obtain what is unlawful. For this reason the apostle Paul ruled against this heresy beforehand, saying: “Nevertheless, in the Lord neither is woman without man nor man without woman.” Far, far be it that women should be shut out everywhere, or that permission should be granted everywhere. They have their proper places: with a husband, with sons, with brothers, with parents, with servants, and in the house of prayer only in the company of all the clergy. But in a single dwelling, where there is no kinship, it is not fitting for them to have companions. This is the balance that hangs level. Whatever tips the balance cannot stand, for Scripture says: “You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left,” and the Lord in the gospel: “Whatever is more than this comes from evil.” Learn now the measure of temperance, you who seek excess through licence. Love women amid the sacred solemnities, and hate them in private companionship, if you wish to hold to Solomon's teaching: “A time to love,” he says, “and a time to hate.”

Partnerships with women, then, are to be guarded against at the times when there is constant, close and frequent dealing in fleshly concerns; for amid its concerns the flesh always stirs up the incitements of desire, and it produces the tinder of sin wherever, busy with the advantages of this temporal life, it feels itself loosened a little by such thoughts. As Solomon asserts: “The earthly thought weighs down the mind that ponders many things.” But in the assembly of the sacred rites, where the Spirit rules, the handmaid, knowing her place, loses the use of her pleasure and loses her wantonness as well, while heavenly things are being handled and the holy mysteries are being celebrated. The whole of human nature is taken up there, where all things are not human but divine; where veneration, or terror and trembling, strikes every mind, the fleshly substance is surely buried. Even amid the very traffic of the flesh many neglect bodily pleasure: when the legions practise their exercises of arms [?], or the forum rings with lawsuits, or the lecture halls resound with letters, or merchants apply themselves intently to trade, or craftsmen are bent over their crafts. How much more where what is carried on is not the fleshly work of men but the spiritual work of angels? Assaults can do nothing there, where even the demons give way, where no difference of sex at all is allowed to be considered, where neither age nor rank but equality alone reigns. To put it more fully, all there take on such a mind that even marriage itself is forgotten, where Christ speaks, is heard, is attended to, and is himself alone everything, through all and in all, as the apostle testifies, saying: “Where there is neither Jew nor Greek, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, male nor female, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.” It is plainly a glory to celebrate this assembly with women, an assembly in which there is no distinction of condition, and in which it is allowed to make all so equal, without any difference, that not even in baptism is anyone ashamed of nakedness; for there the infancy of Adam and Eve is renewed, and one does not put off a garment but rather receives one.

But if even there someone worse than the devil is wounded by the sight of women, our congregation is not to blame for anyone, since it gathers for the sake of heavenly things, not earthly ones. If anyone there is shameless with lustful gazes, let him look to himself; he in no way harms another who has come forward for salvation not to a human being but to Christ. Indeed, I will shut out the objectors with their own objections, so that they yield not to my propositions but to their own. If the common assembly can be made to stumble during the sacred feasts, where the tempter, the devil himself, trembles, who can promise himself to stand firm there where the tempter boldly confronts him? And if we are in danger there, where God's commands gather us together, what will become of us where God's orders keep us apart? And if we are troubled there, where we are fortified by God's will, how much more where we have not only the devil but the Lord too against us? For along with his most holy commands divine protection is supplied to us, as Isaiah says: “He gave the law,” he says, “as a help”; but without divine commands there can be no protection.

It is one thing to do what God commands, and another to resist his will. His commands must be kept in such a way that if he orders something that seems unjust by human standards, it is believed to be just and is done; and if he orders what is just, it is reckoned just and is done. For what he commands cannot fail to win, since he has the power to call injustice justice by justifying it, and to prove justice a perverse injustice by rejecting it. His will alone is true justice. If everything we do, we do only to please the Lord, then surely the only just thing will be whatever God, whom we long to please, has willed, commanded and approved. Slaves cannot know by themselves what pleases their masters unless they follow their masters' orders, and indeed men [?]. If men cannot discern the wishes of other men like themselves unless they are told what to observe, then mortals are much less able to grasp the justice of the immortal God, unless he himself deigns to show the signs of what he counts just. Solomon confirms this when he says: "For who among men can know the counsel of God? Or who can conceive what God wills? The thoughts of mortals are timid, and our foresight is uncertain. For the perishable body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that ponders many things. We can hardly guess at what is on earth, and what lies before us we find only with labor; but who will search out what is in heaven? Who knows your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your holy spirit from on high? And so the paths of those on earth were set right, and people learned what pleases you, and were saved through wisdom." Those who walk in darkness cannot show themselves the light unless the light freely offers itself to those who cannot see. In the same way human blindness cannot find its way to God unless he himself shows the lamp of the law. So David says: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." And again: "The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes." Whatever God has made known, then, is what brings light, and what is worthy of God is what God himself declares acceptable to his will, so that he may exercise his lordship in all things. Otherwise we would not be counted as servants, nor would he be held to be Lord, if we were allowed to serve according to our own will and to choose the exercises of justice by our own judgment rather than God's. The apostle Paul shows the emptiness of such people when he says: "Not knowing God's justice and wishing to establish their own, they did not submit to God's justice." So let these empty evasions and pointlessly slanderous complaints now be set aside. With God's help we are not afraid to join with women for spiritual acts, for we believe that in doing so we are acting justly by God's command, and we know that this provides us with protection. But in private the dwellings of continent clergy and of virgins must be kept as separate as possible, because what God judges wrong cannot be right. Living together, even if no shameful practice is known to occur there, still sets the fire burning, because an integrity that fights against God's commands cannot possibly win. As much as the law gives help to the obedient, so much does it stir up the disobedient, indeed it stirs up sin, as the apostle says: "The power of sin is the law." So the one who commanded us to triumph alongside women in his sacred rites is the same one who commands us to beware of battles with women in private.

There are, to be sure, other necessities that compel us to see women in private as well, but these too are imposed by the force of a divine command or work: that we visit them, offer comfort, and give them life-giving encouragement for their salvation. Yet even in these duties no less care must be taken over our conduct, so that the marks of purity shine out in what we do. Let there be no lack of the strictness that keeps a woman restrained in the presence of a cleric, so that she receives even our consolation with trembling and feels the kindness of the visit in such a way that she reveres the cleric. Not to delay by going through every detail: whatever we do can be honorable if the marks of honor always shine out in us. The apostle Paul summed up everything when he said: "Let all your things be done decently." And again: "As we instructed you, walk honorably." Nothing done carelessly turns out well, and a holy act is not holy unless what is holy is carried out in a holy way, as Solomon declares: "Those who keep just things justly will be made just." Sincerity itself, then, must be kept sincerely, and everything that belongs to the vow must also be marked out in action, lest the vows commend one thing and the actions suggest another. The purpose of the will must be proved in every respect, and the course of every contest must be completed in every respect, lest something be lacking for the triumph because the fight was not fought to the full. So the apostle Paul brings in lessons from the games: "Whoever competes in a contest is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules." And again: "Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may win it. Everyone who competes in the games exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one." This, then, is the fullness of holiness and the perfect palm: to keep nothing at all beside oneself that one has renounced, lest by holding on to what one professes to hate one seem to love it.

But if someone says, "I hold my adversary captive, so that I may always triumph over him," let him take care that the captive does not begin to get the better of him. A thief shut in with treasure is never safe to leave, nor is a lamb safe living in one cage with a wolf. Whoever has led his own enemy inside his gates has chosen to be breached, and whoever has opened his dwelling to his adversary has set a sword in his own bowels. Whoever trusts himself to live alongside a stumbling block says in vain, "I want to be at peace with the devil," against the apostle, who says: "Do not give place to the devil." So the place where treasure has been hidden must be fortified in every way, lest the thief undermine the whole wall through a single hole. If, attacking from outside, he is barely kept off by the walls, how strong will he be once he has been given a dwelling within them? And if those who shut him out are sometimes captured by him, how much more the one who freely opened the way in to him, since Solomon says: "If the just man is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?" So every crack, not to say every gate, must be shut, lest the whole camp be penetrated through a single hole, and all the defenses must be set in order, lest the whole city fall through one small unfortified place. As Solomon says again: "Whoever despises small things will fall little by little."

I am astonished at the perverse judgment by which clergy choose a woman rather than a man to share their lives. Is a woman really as useful for a cleric's needs as a continent man, or a boy, is to a continent man? Or will usefulness be seemly when it comes from an unseemly partnership? And what becomes of Solomon's saying: "Every animal loves its like"? And again: "Birds flock to their like." Even if a woman were thought more useful, carnal advantages should not have been put ahead of spiritual benefits. It would have been better to put up with a man, however useless, to protect one's reputation, than to have a woman's good services at the price of a most shameful reputation. Solomon makes the comparison when he says: "Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman who does good." The devil's favors, then, are always contrived. Through them he exercises his cunning, helping those devoted to holiness with deceitful conveniences in order to destroy them. Among the continent he supplies what look like necessary benefits through mutual help, and he first drives a man and a woman to [live] together, so that, once he has made them inseparable through comforting each other, he can kill those who bring simple hearts to keeping their vows of chastity. Meanwhile he lays aside the weapons of his attack and, like a gentle supporter, suggests arguments for holiness, until over a long time he has nursed a hostile friendship between the two. He makes them friendly to each other and eager to serve each other. A hostile flatterer, he removes every obstacle and delights in making their comforts succeed, so that, binding them to each other through every need, he can present them as dependent on each other for their accustomed consolation. He does not want to hinder them in anything, lest he separate them, whether spiritually or carnally. He makes them live undisturbed, lest at too early a stage something should upset the bonds formed at the very beginning of their partnership. He invites, cherishes and lifts them up toward the perfection of holiness, with everything provided for, to such a degree that they count as God's favors the very things that harm them and lead them to perish, not knowing that God never helps what he forbids. The devil flatters them and builds up such confidence in their holiness that they think they stand firmer against lust together than apart. He leads them on in perfect calm, troubling them with no storms or waves, and, as if in the middle of the sea, he induces them, now less careful, to slacken the sails and neglect the helm, so that he may stir up a sudden tempest and sink them, shipwrecked by an upheaval they never expected. At first he shows this gentleness to lure two ships into coming together, so that once he has joined them he can dash them against each other with sudden whirlwinds and break them. He uses these enticements, withdrawing all his darts, holding back adversity and supplying prosperity, and he keeps the fire smoldering out of sight with no flames until he can join two torches and set both alight at once. He refrains from bringing up the weapons of his savagery until, like a skilled hunter, he has bound what he means to kill in the cords of his snare. But once he has them fast in an unbreakable chain, he at once forces the two, like a trainer with two gladiators, to arm against each other. Goading their limbs, he immediately fits them with swords, immediately kindles their madness, and, thrusting them into wounding embraces, kills both at once with a single blow. So he unfolds what he seemed earlier to be granting; so out of simple charity he forges unlawful love; so through holiness he slips in destruction. By being content to give way, he is able to seize more firmly; by humbly allowing himself to appear defeated, he boasts of a more complete victory. The apostle Paul understands his tricks when he says: "For we are not ignorant of his wiles." So those whom the devil leads into war by making peace have made a bad peace in this partnership. Those whose very progress the enemy craftily arranges for their ruin do not advance well in holiness. Nor do they climb the ladder of continence by a straight course whom the adversary labors to draw up to the summit so that he may hurl them down from the height. Those who have kept to a slippery road are bound to be dashed down in their fall. Of this road Solomon declares: "There is a way that seems right to men, but its end leads into the depths of hell."

But they say: "If clergy are censured for this kind of union, then many saints must be censured along with us: whether Elijah, who stayed with a widow; or the apostles, who took women around with them as companions, like John, who took in the Lord's mother when the Lord himself entrusted her to him; or the Lord himself, whom certain devout women supported from their own means, whom Martha served at table, who sat by the well and spoke alone with a foreign woman of Samaria, and whose feet, as he reclined at table, a woman washed with her tears and wiped with her hair." Clever arguers and deceitful lawyers! In their eagerness to evade the law, they twist even the laws themselves in disputes and lawsuits. Unwilling to be bound by the commands of the laws that apply to them, they put forward unsuitable precedents, as if they were comparable legal arguments, to make fools of the judges. They are exposed through Solomon by the wisdom of the law itself: "A sinful man," he says, "avoids correction and finds a comparison to suit his will." Such people, then, must first be refuted not by argument but by correction, so that they are not instructed by explanations before they have lost what they found to prop up their defense. Solomon teaches us how to deal with people of this kind when he says: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him; but answer a fool against his folly, so that he may not seem wise to himself."

Great men indeed, who compare themselves to the saints, and what an outstanding way of life we have, that it should seem equal to the prophets or the apostles! We are not willing to imitate the saints except perversely, as a pretext for our self-indulgence, and in our other actions we are not willing to follow in the footsteps of the righteous. In some things we excuse ourselves as too weak to imitate the deeds of our forebears, while in others we declare ourselves their equals. Yet Elijah himself, when he was in distress, confessed before God that he was not equal to his fathers: "Am I better than my fathers?" Elijah in his weakness is driven to cry this out about those who went before him, and we do not hesitate to make our virtue equal to that of Elijah, the prophets, the apostles and the Lord? Clearly I see greed trampled underfoot among us, just as the apostles left everything they owned! I see gluttony and drunkenness as absent from our banquets as hunger was present to the apostles, who had nothing and were often forced to go without food! I recognize that fasting, thirst, hunger and nakedness, endured for the sake of urgent teaching alone, flourish everywhere among us, just as we read that they triumphed in the apostles! It is plain that among us the same exercises of virtue burn brightly that made all the vices tremble before the apostles! Clearly we practise the Lord's forty-day fast, and the prayers and vigils with which he broke even the silence of the night in desert places! Do we take part in similar contests against the assaults of the vices? Do we act with such rigor, authority, vigils, sufferings, labor, hardship, affliction and abstinence, by which sins are trampled down, that no one suspects us of anything evil? It is through these that the apostle Paul boasts that his conscience had been made known to all: "In all things commending ourselves as ministers of God: in much endurance, in pressures, in tribulations, in hardships, in distresses, in beatings, in custody, in prisons, in riots, in prayers, in labors, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, with the weapons of justice on the right hand and on the left." For imitating these things we are weak, but for taking women around with us we claim the ability to match their example. Even if someone boasted that he had fulfilled everything they did, no one's persuasion could bring me to believe that there are other apostles now, against the declaration of the apostle Paul: "Are all apostles? Are all prophets?" If Christ, who said, "The Father is greater than I," dared to compare himself with God, or if the apostles dared to make themselves equal to Christ, then let a like strength make us equal to the apostles today! Wretched humanity, are you not afraid of being struck by lightning for claiming such equality, you who do not hesitate to borrow from the Son of God or from the sons of thunder examples supposedly like your own sins? It is the swollen boasting of pride for anyone to want to be counted comparable even to the least in the church, since Paul warns: "Each regarding the other as better than himself." And further on he adds: "Have this mind among you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant."

We should certainly think less highly of our own strength, and our weakness must not be compared with the fortitude of the saints. The apostle Paul sets himself before us as a lesson when he says: "For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves; rather, we commend ourselves by our own standard, not boasting beyond measure but according to the measure of glory that God has measured out to us." But if we consider what he also said, "I labored more than all of them," nothing better or more fitting is offered me to win the case than to answer the objection with the very man on whose authority it is raised against me. Certainly he labored more than all, and yet he shrank in fear from imitating his colleagues in taking women around with him, lest he expose himself rashly to carnal temptation. He gave his reason himself when he said: "I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air; but I punish my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be found disqualified." Compare yourself with him, then, you who boast of being an apostle, and learn from him what you should fear, for he cries out: "I beg you, be imitators of me." So he refused to feel confident about taking women around with him, for he knew how much some virtues differ from others; drawing a comparison with the gifts of the church, he had declared that the sun has one glory, the moon another, and the stars another. But we, on the contrary, flatter ourselves that we are equal to the apostles, without paying any real attention to what the apostles and all the saints did by their invincible virtue. We try to force our way along a difficult road when a smoother one across easy ground has been set before us, against Solomon, who says: "Do not trust yourself to a toilsome road, lest you set a stumbling block for your soul." Nor does anyone consider that one man walks safely on slippery ground while another, who is not up to it, slips; one runs up mountains over the crags while another, if he strains himself, falls; one manages to bring his ships safely through storms, while another cannot meet with such good fortune. The apostle Paul settles this when he says: "Each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and another of another."

But those who use the example of the saints to prejudge the case against me: why will they not consider another example that should make them afraid? And why does the man who strives to be made equal to the apostles not rather set before himself, as a warning, the adulterous elders in Daniel? I do not put this forward to contradict those who imitate the apostles, but to confound those who make themselves equal to the saints. Nor do I deny that we must follow those whom we have all received as teachers. My quarrel is with those who want to twist the stories of good men to serve their own wrongdoing and think that the law supports them. Like all who are hurrying to their ruin, they want their disgraceful conduct concealed under the cover of the saints, and under the pretense of imitating their forebears they commit everything contrary to them. The apostle Paul exposes them and makes them known when he says: "What I do I will go on doing, to cut off the opportunity from those who want an opportunity, so that in what they boast of they may be found to be just as we are. For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ." To heap their ruin still higher, they defame the good men whose example they use for evil. It would be quite useful and wholesome for them to believe that they had failed to understand the meaning of some story, rather than to suppose that there was anything dishonorable in the law. The apostle Paul confounds and rebukes them when he says: "Understanding neither what they are saying nor the things about which they make assertions." And again: "If anyone thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know." So the prejudgments of these impudent people are void. The wayward ingenuity of their perversity leads them astray; they look for stories to expound that suit their own notions, and in their wrongdoing they borrow the law's protection. But to those who do right, everything that is written is good, for they take what is well said in a good sense, as the apostle Paul assures us: "We know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully."

We have prevailed by confounding our opponents. Now we turn to instructing as well those whom we have defeated, so that we neither leave the saints under accusation nor are thought incapable of giving an account. Having been publicly defeated, they may then repent; or, if they refuse, we have at least discharged what our diligence requires. Just as we have satisfied the saying of Solomon quoted above, we may then also satisfy the apostle Paul when he declares: "The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, apt to teach, patient, correcting with all modesty those who resist, in case God may grant them repentance to know the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will."

Everything our forebears did was done for a reason, so that authority, fortified on every side, might be handed down to us who came after them, for use against transgressors. To forestall the heresy we censured above, the Lord relaxed things a little in the matter of receiving women, whether in his own person or through his servants, so that his handiwork should not be condemned altogether through excessive rigour. The Lord foresaw the heretics who abolish marriage and who strive, against the first principle of nature and against the gospel, to separate those whom the Lord has joined. To forbid them, an authority was already being prepared then, so that married women should not be barred from approaching Christ, whom they served while he was present. But even this permission was not arranged without restraint, for what he did, he did not for himself but for others. For if the Lord spoke with the Samaritan woman, he taught her for an hour and went away, and he offered no defence for prolonged excesses. For an hour, too, he allowed Martha to serve him. But what else was this for the Lord than serving up the banquets of the heavenly kingdom? Were there no feasts in the Lord's company? Or in the presence of his majesty was there any other food or drink than the teaching alone that nourished them? The Lord himself bears witness to this when he says: "My food is to do the will of him who sent me." In the same way the company of women accompanied the apostles, not to ruin them but to learn reverence, and they followed in order to render a service of human kindness, as the gospel records of the Lord and of them alike: "And it came to pass after these things," it says, "that he himself was travelling through cities and villages, preaching the good news of the kingdom of God, and the twelve were with him, and women who had been healed of unclean spirits and infirmities: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, who ministered to him from their own means."

Did they cling to one another one by one, man to woman? Did they persist in an undisciplined cohabitation, living together in an enticing companionship? No: almost the whole church could see that they followed him not for shameless banquets but to learn the practices of a good life. So little is described there that could be compared with our banquets that no laughter and no joking is said to have been present. Nor is it said, as still happens in some places today, that a choir of virgins singing psalms soothed anyone's ears with poisonous songs. And to show briefly how much loose familiarity could displease the apostles: were they not driven to have doubts even about the Lord himself when he spoke with a woman, and would they not have voiced them had their proven knowledge of his majesty not restrained them? As the evangelist reports: "Meanwhile," he says, "his disciples came, and they marvelled that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said to him, 'What do you seek?' or 'Why are you speaking with her?'" And what shall I say of the woman who approached and threw herself at the Lord's feet, whose weeping and lamenting the shameless do not blush to claim in defence of their own wantonness? Their own blindness carries them so far that they cannot hold back even from comparisons like these. Of such people Solomon says: "Their malice blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God." John, it is true, appears to have taken in the Lord's mother. But she was a mother whose character the name "mother" itself declares. Yet I cannot admit other mothers of Christ as well, and she who bore the Majesty is not to be put on a level with all women. Elijah too was commanded by the Lord to leave the wilderness and enter a widow's dwelling. At the Lord's command he endured staying in a house, he to whom the wilderness was a palace for his rest. The Lord gave him the occasion to perform mighty works, so that in time of famine he might instead provide sufficient food to the widow and her orphans. He had been worn down everywhere by fasting and had endured want, and he had come because he was sent to be fed; yet instead it was he who brought food [?] to the wretched and drove out the miseries of their want. This cannot support anyone's laxity, since there was no opportunity for scandal: he was only passing through, and, worse still, the lodging he had was so destitute that any guest would have fled it. And yet he finished his task among those who gave him lodging and went back, and even if he had stayed longer he could not have come under suspicion. What sort of affection could there be in sharing a life where there was no food? And what sort of access to the widow did Elijah have, when it was famine that gave him lodging? Whoever you are who wish to be called a disciple of Elijah because he stayed with the widow, first endure the hardships of the wilderness and a fast of forty days, and either you will not look for a woman, or there will be no one left alive to stay with a woman. And even then, if you have the strength, keep watch over yourself. To us, however, the angel and the Lord Christ point to no one else but John alone as having come in the spirit and power of Elijah.

Shame! We are forced to grieve over what we teach, since we have come to this: we are discussing the awesome virtues of the saints in comparison with the dissolute. Spare us now, spare us, impudence! The saints never side with you, for whatever dealings they had with women were religious, modest, venerable, chaste and decent. Or if you still strive to hunt out twisting paths of quibbling through the saints, we know that the friends of God are to be mentioned only with veneration, as David taught when he said: "But to me your friends, O God, are greatly honoured." Let the robbers of modesty and kidnappers of chastity go now and lay out their troubles and complaints to their silly women. Among our saints they have no refuge at all, and by the authority of the apostle Paul the church is forbidden to mix with them. "And avoid these," he says, "for of these are those who creep into houses and lead captive silly women laden with sins, who are led away by various desires."

After this decree, let them go on trusting, if they like, that the examples of the angels help their case. They can no longer sway us, for we know that angels too fell with women. They do well, indeed, to borrow their patronage from those angels, but we hear of no angel against the apostle Paul. "But even if we," he says, "or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than the one we preached to you, let him be anathema." All who do not yield to this prohibition are utterly mad and burn with the fire of women. Gaping after obscenities, they would rather die than be content to be torn from women's sides by any separation at all. To satisfy the filth of their greed, they cannot be without the pleasure of a woman even for a moment. This is the fruit they get from women: with their attention ever fixed on them, they glut the desires of their eyes, so that not a single moment passes in which they lack what they crave. So integrity dies among them, where every form of living together, whether eating together or dwelling together, is polluted by corrupt affections. Saint Peter had pointed them out, saying: "Revelling in their feasts, having eyes full of adultery and of sins that never cease, enticing unstable souls." Solomon too marks them out: "An abomination before the Lord," he says, "is he who fixes his eye." Job plainly testifies that he keeps himself pure against his eye when he says: "and if my heart has consented to my eyes." A man can indeed be held free of guilt in his eyes if, against his will, a sudden encounter with a woman has stirred a temptation which his mind immediately drives out, because it did not want it. But a man does not deserve to escape the disturbance of his sight if he keeps the material of temptation in his own house, if he wants to enjoy gazing with desire, if he seeks to have what thrusts offence upon his eyes. Amid constant stumbling blocks the insatiable greed of the eyes can in no way be restrained, as Solomon confirms when he says: "Hell and destruction are never satisfied; so the eyes of men are insatiable." And in another place: "The eye is not satisfied with seeing." And again: "What has been created more wicked than the eye?"

Not stung by this rebuke, they despise the divine prohibitions with an obstinate attachment to their unspeakable familiarity, and on top of that they still plead charity. As Isaiah says, they swallow bitterness for sweetness and cover naked foulness with the veil of a good name, so that among them true love is violated under the guise of false love. But Charity cries out and appeals: "I did not join such people together; let that other one go, the one who counterfeits me by pretence. I never resist God's commandments, I never favour the dissolute, and I do not want holiness to be blamed because of me. A hostile brotherhood slanders me, and I too have run into perils among false brethren. Help me, my herald, help me, apostle Paul! Bear witness for me, so that what you proclaim of me may not be perverted: 'The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned.'" Is that to be counted as love, which lays holiness open to injury and accusation? Or is their brotherhood to be thought sincere, when through them the daughters of mother church are led into guilt? If such a thing is reckoned Christian charity, then without doubt hatreds are better, for when they separate people they stain no one. But this parricidal love habitually unites brothers who are persecutors, who willingly let the daughters of the church be defamed as fornicators because of their companionship. This goes against the charity which the apostle Paul taught when he said: "Love of neighbour works no evil." A splendid proof of charity indeed, which not only harms its neighbour through a noxious brotherhood but also refuses to be subject to the rules of the apostolic command! Let the champions of such love be put to shame. They stand judged by those who abandon even the love of their own blood for the common good.

Almost the whole human race throughout the world is joined by ties of kinship, and everywhere natural relatives are separated as one or another goes abroad. Parents can do it, children can do it, brothers can do it, and, what is more, even husbands and wives can break the bonds of nature that God has granted them. Yet clerics, when God does not grant it and even forbids it, are unable to give up a charity enslaved to the ties of women? The ever-cherished closeness of near kin is absent from relatives, and clerics resist being kept apart from women who are strangers to them? They ought to have done this even if the Lord had commanded something peculiar or unusual, since they have the Holy Spirit for accomplishing the impossible, which worldly men do not have. Hence the apostle John admonishes them: "Little children, overcome them, because he who is in you is greater than he who is in this world." But as things are, what is possible even for the Gentiles, to say nothing of Christians, and is regarded as light, is emptied of all effect among clerics. It is not enough for them to despise God's commandments; they must have another disgrace besides: they do not even keep up with the custom of all the nations, let alone surpass it. The Lord reproaches them through Ezekiel and says: "You have not walked in my statutes and have not carried out my judgments, nor have you even acted according to the judgments of the nations round about you." This love must mean something shameful, since they think it against nature to have it wrested from them.

I have something more to marvel at. I see many Christians, husbands and wives alike, who have resolved on continence and choose separate dwellings instead, so that by a harmonious withdrawal, without the provocation of each other's presence, they may keep the agreement of their common vows. And our eunuchs cannot bear to sleep without a woman's company? Among the former, married love is outweighed by love of continence, while among the eunuchs living with a woman can never become tiresome. Let the charity of the eunuchs speak now, let it speak: perhaps it is rather married charity that sins by this separation, so that the apostle Paul's counsel seems to have suggested divorce to married people: "The time that remains," he says, "is short. It remains that even those who have wives should be as though they had none." What perversity of love is at work, when those who have wives strive to be as though they had none, and those who have none boast of being as though they had! Of these the apostle himself says: "Their glory is in their shame."

"It is love," they say. O love that begrudges itself! O charity that longs to be praised by being reproached! It is a great marvel that the charity of virgins makes virgins be taken for married people, and the charity of married people makes married people be thought virgins. Here is true love, which divides in marriage in order to unite in chastity! Here is holy love, which leads married people to live apart for the praise of both! These certainly love each other inseparably, who part from each other to win triumphs for themselves. Neither crime nor nature nor law nor the Lord nor the apostle forbade them or took away from them the right to share one life; but charity persuaded them to live apart, setting aside their unity of heart to protect the vows they had made together. But let the others consider whose charity it is that they know, who yield neither to crime nor to nature nor to law nor to the Lord nor to the apostle nor even to marriage itself. A disgraceful virginity condemns them as much as a castrated marriage glorifies those others. Let it be punishment and disgrace enough for them that eunuchs are judged by married people. To rebuke them, we must not pass over in silence the children of Israel either, who in the time of Ezra did not hesitate to drive away the wives and children they had taken against divine law, nor did they try to make excuses against the love of the Lord. Let me speak the truth, if I may. These men, who now cling together rather than send away women who are not their own, what would they do if they were ordered to cast off their children and wives? Or when will they be able to renounce their kin for Christ, when they put silly women who are not even theirs ahead of Christ's commandments? I say that they would more easily disown their own parents for the sake of those same silly women than be able to leave those silly women for Christ's sake. They despise what the Lord himself declared in the gospel: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father or mother or wife and children and brothers and sisters, and his own life, he cannot be my disciple."

If those who hesitate to cast off their parents are unworthy of Christ, what can men promise themselves who are shown to be despisers of Christ by something that is not even affection for their parents? And so they are put to nothing by the merits of those whom they see making no exception of any of their kin for the sake of Christ. They are shamed no less, indeed even more, by those who, afraid of having to wrestle not only with another's flesh but even with their own, cut off their genitals and so castrate themselves. Concerning these I suspend judgment for now, leaving the matter to be set out in another discussion. But to shame our eunuchs I do not hesitate to declare those men better, who do not spare even themselves, let alone dare to hold out temptations to women. Let the spiritual eunuchs answer: what madness is there in the love of women, or what mystery in sharing quarters with a woman, that they indulge members not their own to their own destruction, when those men cut off even their own without hesitation? Those men cast away limbs firmly set in their own bodies, while these glue themselves to members that are their adversaries. Those men do not hesitate to fight for spiritual integrity at the cost of the torment of a body no longer whole, while these, without any torment, refuse to be whole without their female half. But no comparison should be drawn between our own people and these men, lest those who stand condemned by any Christian judgment take comfort from it. Others who are worse must also be mentioned, so that the penalty may be greater, to be condemned by the condemned. Let them consider the Jews, who to this day, at the command of the law, cut off part of their flesh by the torment of circumcision, and let them learn what they deserve who, though the gospel commands it, neglect to do the Lord's will by being circumcised from the presence of women. They do not understand that the Lord himself said: "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." I suppose the idolaters too may reproach us and taunt us with their Galli, who castrate themselves and willingly torture themselves, so long as, at the cost of their own condition, they may obey the sham rites of their idols. But our clerics prefer, for the gain of their own bodies, to put up with the harm of women living with them, women they ought to tear out even from their own substance if they happened to be born joined to them, so as not to blush when compared with idolaters and sacrilegious men. Of such people the Lord also rebuked those who despise him, saying: "The children of this world are wiser than the children of light." So the profane devotion of such men is to be preferred to our clerics, for they hold their shameful priesthoods dear at the price of such great ruin. Our clerics, however, for the dignity of a heavenly priesthood shed no blood and endure no steel; there is no wound, there is no torture. The mere sight of a woman alone sets them burning against the Lord. They rush upon women in such a way and love women in such a way that they do not expect the "pure mysteries" of their love ever to be brought to light, though they have been shamefully published and laid bare through men like them. These the apostle Paul had already foreseen even then, when he said: "The sins of some men are manifest, going before them to judgment, and some men's sins follow after them. Likewise good deeds too are manifest, and those that are otherwise cannot be hidden."

But they in turn say: "Some of our [?], who likewise kept women in their houses, attained martyrdom, which proved that their conscience was innocent." I do not want anyone to bring martyrdom against me as an argument, because adulterers, murderers, drunkards and men guilty of every crime have often been converted when an occasion for combat arose and have deserved to attain the pardon of martyrdom. Indeed, martyrdom is called both a crown and a baptism because it baptizes and crowns at once. Come now: if some were allowed to earn martyrdom while their companionship with women remained unbroken, then martyrdom was not without pardon for them either. The guilt of forbidden cohabitation did not leave them acquitted, and martyrdom could not prove them innocent in that very innocence of theirs; rather, it is seen to have forgiven them their contempt of the law, the foulness of their illicit way of life, and, what is gravest of all, their crime against the church. For an innocence that harms the good name of Christ's bride is a guilty innocence. Christ, the innocent Lamb, or rather, to speak more truly, heavenly innocence itself, gave up his whole self for the church, so that he might present her untouched, without any spot or wrinkle. What kind of cleric, then, is he to whom the bride of Christ is entrusted, if he lets the whole church be blamed for love of a single woman? I would dare to say this: the Son was sent by God the Father from the Father's bosom and endured being absent from his kingdom in order to make the church innocent, and a cleric cannot leave a woman's side to keep Christ's church from disgrace?

But they say: "In martyrdom we are forgiven, as our fathers were pardoned." Then let all of us trust in this for all our sins! Let us who toil to do good wander about among luxuries and run up and down the paths of sin; let us drop the reins and slacken the bridles. Let us go wherever the world carries us off and wherever the devil invites us; let us freely fornicate, envy, rob, defraud; let us commit every evil without a care: martyrdom will come to our aid and we will escape. For that is what the apostle Paul promises: "Let us do evil that good may come"; their condemnation is just. Let those pin their hope on this martyrdom who have been taught by the astrologers to foreknow tomorrow, and let those expect these crowns who, above the angels and Christ, have learned through astrologers to know the times which the Father has set in his own authority. Then at least they may remember that they ought to have done good before the time of martyrdom, when they perceive the day of the Lord coming like a thief. But let us suppose that martyrdom is already hanging over them at any moment. Meanwhile, before they become martyrs, they are subject to the laws and so are subject to judgment, unless they are stripped of their weapons [?]. It is an outrage of audacity for them to set the persons of their fathers against the authority of the Lord, for the Lord himself has silenced this objection: "Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers," he says, "and do not keep their judgments, and do not mingle in their pursuits, and do not be defiled. I am the Lord your God. Walk in my commandments and keep my judgments."

Let them know now that the patronage of their fathers has been taken from them, these men who run back and forth looking for hiding places of argument so that they may never be without women. Deserted on every side by anything that might support their defence, they finally, with all their arguments exhausted, imagine that a saying of the apostle Paul comes to their aid, and they say: "Who are you to judge another's servant?" Paul does indeed recognize the words of his own ruling that they cite, but he does not know the men who invoke and cite it. For he gave that defence to those who attack no part of the law, and he granted that protection to those who do something by their own free choice and obstruct nothing of the church's law. He is dealing with the freedom [?] to eat and not to eat, confirming each person's own choice. In such matters he commanded that no one should be judged, because divine authority left them to each person's will and kindly allowed both doing and not doing. But he made subject to the church's tribunals those transgressors of the established order whom no impunity excused. So let those who everywhere bring forward "Who are you to judge another's servant?" against us, like a written counter-plea, recognize the reasoned and certain rejoinder that we have received from the same apostle Paul: "We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw from brothers who walk in a disorderly way and not according to the tradition you received from us."

We have escaped, I think, the great tangle of questions in which the embraces of women have bound eunuchs who are lovers. These men are driven to twist the decrees of the law with perverse interpretations, and would rather be heard putting forward vain and fabulous inventions than listen to what is true themselves. The apostle Paul foretold them when he said: “They will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn aside to fables.” Let them go on searching out whatever they like in order to resist the truth on behalf of women. They win no victory, these people for whom, contrary to Ezra, woman has triumphed rather than truth. But you, dearest sons, I address not only with persuasion but also with authority. Despise this madness. You know that the apostle Paul everywhere condemned the disputes of such men, as he wrote to the Romans: “I beg you, brothers, to watch carefully those who say or do things that cause dissensions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching you have learned, and turn away from them.” So too he charges Timothy: “Do not quarrel about words,” he says, “for it does no good, but only ruins those who hear. Take care to present yourself to God as one approved, a workman beyond reproach, rightly handling the word of truth.
