But avoid foolish and empty talk, for it leads on greatly to ungodliness, and their talk spreads like a cancer.” And to show those who order the clergy what teaching is fitting for doing away with such disputes, he also instructs Titus: “But you, speak what befits sound doctrine: that the older men be sober, prudent, sound in faith, in love, and in sincere patience.” Let your obedience, then, take in plain teaching, and shun the shifty deceit of contradictions. Clear a clean path for your steps, and do not tread upon thorns and thistles, lest the good seed be unable to bring you the fruit of holiness because of the thorny thickets. That is why the prophet Jeremiah exhorts and teaches us: “Do not sow among thorns,” he says. “Circumcise yourselves to your God; circumcise the foreskin of your heart.” So everything that habitually pricks and tears must be cut out of your field, lest the farmer’s mind become entangled in malignant briars on his own land. And we must cut away everything that the furnace of seething flesh throws up as it boils over, teeming with the sulphurous flames of fiery tinder, lest even a tiny spark left behind kindle a greater blaze. Solomon makes this plain when he says: “From a single spark a fire grows.” Turn away from the impure occasions by which the inner depths of the heart are penetrated, so that a clear transparency may be honored in you. Be content to endure a laborious single life for the sake of preserving your chastity, rather than to arrive at disgrace without labor.

Consider what it means to preside over a holy people, and reflect on what it is to attend upon the divine sacraments. Those who live by the altar must be pleasing to the altar, and those who are consecrated ought to have a care for purity that matches the sacred things to which they render the duties of their service, lest they themselves give offense to the Lord in what they handle, or begin to hinder among the people what they preach. That is why the apostle Paul testifies and says: “We endure all things, so as not to put any obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.” And again: “Giving no offense to anyone, so that our ministry may not be blamed.” By this rule, then, you must labor as hard as you can regarding those for whom singleness, rather than living in pairs, is the true witness to make their seriousness plain. Look at how many evils this companionship of pairs brings with it. It sows nothing but corruption; it sprouts vices, conceives desire, gives birth to disgrace, stirs up rage, spreads frenzy, feeds lewdness, nourishes wantonness, exalts falls, builds ruins; it raises steep banks, lays out precipices, sails into dangers, sets its course for shipwreck, rejoices in perdition, cherishes destruction, buys confusion, hoards reproach, heaps up charges, inflames accusations; and gathering all together at once into one bundle, it heaps up countless snares of entrapment and brings manifold deaths through endless disgraces to the ruin of the lost.

So many and such great ravages of calamity and of the worst way of life no one overthrows, no one tramples, no one lays in the grave, except single chastity alone. It is the unconquered fortress of holiness and the strong assault upon infamy; the firmness of fortitude and the weakness of wanton lust; the bulwark of uprightness and the destruction of wickedness; the victory of the soul and the plunder of the body; the abundance of glories and the captivity of crimes; the bridesmaid of holiness and the divorce of shamefulness; the sign of purity and the abolition of scandals; the exercise of continence and the complete emptying of lust; the secure peace of the virtues and the quiet conquest of wars; the summit of purity and the prison of lust; the harbor of honor and the place where disgrace is shipwrecked; the mother of virginity and the enemy of uncleanness; the breastplate of modesty and the stripping of shamelessness; the death of corruption; the wall of strictness and the destruction of vulgarity; the sword of severity, the conqueror and slayer of dissoluteness; the armor of strength and the disarming of indulgence; the dignity of integrity and the condemnation of fornication; the pinnacle of renown and the precipice of disgrace; the will for good works and the affliction of vices; the refreshment of modesty and the punishment of wantonness; the acquisition of triumphs and the loss of crimes; the rest of salvation and the exile of perdition; the life of the spirit and the death of the flesh; the state of angelic nature, the funeral of human substance. By its reins all obscenity is curbed, and by its fetters the heels of raging lust are held fast. Against it, as against a rock, every surge of the flooding blood is broken, and in it the foaming madness of bodily swelling is calmed. Since it withdraws from itself every support of desire, it is known to carry members that are dead, of which the apostle Paul gives warning when he says: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are on earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry; on account of these the wrath of God comes.”

From all these things human nature is castrated only by the gleaming knife of singleness, so that by a circumcision that betroths it, it may lead unblemished eunuchs into the banquet of holiness. To it holiness has promised the wedding seal of its ring in such a way that without it virginity is broken open. Singleness, content with itself alone, tames desire and makes the mind chaste; it subdues concupiscence, quenches burning longings, weakens the limbs, enslaves the body, and so crucifies the things of the flesh that both male and female seem in their way of life to belie their sex, since it cuts them off from the activity of either sex. Or rather, making them neither, it boasts of bestowing on both a third form out of the two, so that before the resurrection it is seen to rehearse the image of the resurrection after the likeness of the angels. The Lord promises this for the future when he says: “Those who are counted worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they will not die any more; for they are like the angels of God, since they are children of the resurrection.” Holy singleness demands such merits that, even before it is transfigured, it is already seen transfigured into the appearance of angelic brightness; cutting away everything from itself, it despoils all the struggles of desire. Solomon sings its praises when he says: “Better it is to be without children, with glory. For immortality is in its memory, because it is known both with God and with men. When it is present, men imitate it, and they long for it when it has gone away; and crowned forever it triumphs, winning the battle of undefiled contests.”

No one is without children with glory except singleness alone: not only does its own conscience stain it with no filth, but no rumors of suspected companionship bring it into disrepute either. For even if chastity, which is difficult, were to keep a man and a woman together in virginity, it would not have glory, since the very sharing of life can only cloud it with some darkness of shameful suspicion. Singleness, by contrast, is so bright and evident to all that it shows itself pure and shining to everyone in the splendor of its whiteness. Hence the apostle teaches us: “Walk as children of light, for the fruit of light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth, proving what is pleasing to God.” And again: “Do all things without grumbling or hesitation, that you may be blameless and simple, as children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world.” Singleness shines out everywhere in such a way that all unhesitatingly vouch for it, and it so glorifies holiness in itself that it wrings praise even from its enemies. The apostle Paul commands this especially of anyone placed in authority, when he says: “He must also have a good testimony from those outside, so that he may not fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.” Love this, then; hold fast to this, which alone can conquer women. While no desire yet assails your breast, and while your simplicity still remains uncorrupted and at peace, run quickly to the secret protection of singleness, lest later you be unable to escape.

Every approach must be secured in advance against all ambushes, lest the enemy creep up first and fall upon the unwary. It is a saving remedy to forestall rather than be forestalled, and it befits brave men to anticipate rather than be anticipated. Wherever there is foresight, everything opposed to us is frustrated; but where foresight is neglected, everything opposed to us prevails. We struggle before the [?]; we busy ourselves with labor before want arrives. In this way we leave no room for any calamity, since we exercise foresight about times to come. How much more, then, must the calamity of women be forestalled with every precaution, since once its desire is allowed to begin, it never comes to an end at all? Solomon sets out a comparison for it when he says: “Hell, and the love of a woman, and the earth that is not satisfied with water, and fire, do not say, ‘Enough.’” So let everyone who feels secure because he is not yet tempted be afraid. Because nothing is said about him, let him take care that nothing comes to be said. We are human; we carry our frailty in the flesh. So we must surround and gird ourselves on every side with watchful alertness, so that no part of us wavers. We do indeed receive spiritual strength, by which the frailty of our nature is strengthened. But spiritual strength has been granted us so that it may protect the prudent, not the reckless; so that it may defend those who renounce the solicitations of sin, not those who rather plunge themselves into troublesome sins. The Spirit has been given us as a guardian, but to come to the aid of those who turn away from what is contrary, not to favor those who choose it; not to strengthen those who willingly lean toward adversity, but to confirm those who strive to separate themselves from it. For whoever dares to exercise his virtue in dangerous undertakings has no help from the Holy Spirit, who wants no one to be forced to become a hero of his own accord for the sake of deceptive victories. He does not protect such a man; indeed, he abandons the one he recognizes as rushing into dangers to seek triumphs by unlawful means, as he himself already said long ago through Solomon: “He who loves danger will perish in it.”

The power of the Holy Spirit, therefore, is supplied according to his order, not according to our will, and battles succeed according to his plan. No army has ever fallen except one that was thrown headlong, eager to act bravely, and broke through the dispositions of its general or emperor. Much more does he squander a strength doomed to perish who presumes to triumph without the arms of the Spirit’s teaching as his master, since the Spirit says: “Woe to those who do anything by their own presumption, and not through God.”

If, then, you have any confidence in spiritual strength, remember what befits spiritual men; and if you believe that you are waging spiritual warfare, acknowledge that what we teach is not carnal, as the apostle Paul says: “If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge what I write to you.” There is no reason to flatter yourselves with this deceptive persuasion, wanting to move about among the weapons of the shameful because you are spiritual, or thinking yourselves beyond reach because of the dignity of the clerical office. On the contrary, greater conflicts usually befall greater men. The rich are envied more bitterly than the poor, and the savage attacks of robbers trouble not the needy but the wealthy. In battle, enemies go after generals and princes more than common soldiers, and it is the highest peaks that are battered most violently by winds and whirlwinds. Therefore, the more anyone is able to do beyond others, the more let him know that he must fear lest he be diminished in some way. That is why Solomon warns: “Let him who glories in riches fear poverty.” I beg you as much as I can, and beyond what I can, let this be the aim of all clerics: to live in the retreat of an irreproachable single life, so that neither they through women nor women through them may be drawn into shameful mockery. If anyone has a mother or daughter or sister or wife or kinswoman, let him have her in such a way that no maidservant is among them and no outside woman comes in, lest he seem to keep his relatives for this purpose, that on their account he may freely bring other women into his company. But if these relatives cannot do without the service of maids or the companionship of friends, it is better that they move to another dwelling than that, for their sake, persons who are a danger be kept there. For it is humane that the cleric should not deprive them of the women they need, and that they should not defile the cleric through women who are a source of trouble. They can be placed with holy women to live with, provided that no woman stays with the cleric. Not even a plain woman, not even an old woman, who is not a relative, should be specially taken in for household service. For sin is committed more quickly where it can be committed safely without suspicion, especially since to desire no ugliness and no plainness is distasteful or mean; the devil paints it and makes whatever is foul or repulsive seem beautiful.

If anyone, compelled by a journey, lodges with brothers or with strangers where there are women present, let him restrain himself completely, lest he be corrupted by some susceptibility to passion. Let him keep apart and withdrawn, devoting himself to God and to himself, lest he be caught by the devil indoors, and lest he who could not be caught outside, he who escaped his enemies, fall among his own. Let him come into their presence for a short time, for wholesome reasons, and then quickly hasten to leave their sight again. Everywhere presence with women should be tasted, not prolonged; contact with women should be granted only in passing, as though in flight. For always putting oneself forward in their midst is already the beginning of wantonness, and to make a habit of frequent comings and goings among women is to rehearse one’s own ruin. Solomon has laid down a rule for us on this when he says: “Do not linger in the midst of women.” So walk, then, and so act, that the clergy may always stand as a spotless senate of the church. Let severity toward women thrive in us, let authority prevail, let firmness be maintained, let seriousness be revered.

To gather everything together once and for all in conclusion, we read back to you a summary that the apostle Paul gives, reducing it to a concise fullness: “Finally, brothers,” he says, “whatever is true, whatever is chaste, whatever is just, whatever is holy, whatever is lovely, whatever is of good report, if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline, think on these things, which you have received and learned and heard and seen in me. Do these things, and the God of peace and love will be with you.” Amen.
